Q: Azure DevOps nuget restore fails with "Unable to find version 'x.x.x.x' of package" for internal feed package A:

The solution is to set the nuget version to 7.9.0.

Currently the actual version of nuget.

The solution in the YAML file looks like this:

- task: NuGetToolInstaller@1
    displayName: 'Use NuGet 7.9.0'
    inputs:
      versionSpec: 7.9.0
      checkLatest: true

Q: Is fetching std::chrono::steady_clock inside a critical section necessary to theoretically align C++ happens-before with real-time order? A:

The inverted execution is legal but your test can't ever print it nothing in the standard says t_clear runs promptly a conforming implementation can just stall it for an hour so #2 happening before #1 needs no time travel, just a slow thread but trace your guard: time_buy = now() → buy_stock → unlock → clear_stock's lock → join → t_clear_complete = now(). That whole chain is happens-before, and [time.clock.req] says happens-before implies t1 <= t2. So in the inverted execution time_buy <= t_clear_complete, duration <= 0, and your if (duration >= 1h) never fires. The only executions that print anything are the ones where #1 happens-before #2 — and then the mutex forces "empty".

Clocks don't create happens-before; happens-before constrains clocks. So the "time-inverted" execution isn't forbidden, it's just unobservable from inside the program any measurement ordered with the events is required to agree with the logical order. clear/ok can't happen.

Q: when windows service was created A:

You can use Get-Process to see when the service process was started, like so:

Get-Process | select name, starttime

This will get the processid based on the service name:

$myservice = "Spooler"

$starttime = Get-Process -id ((Get-WmiObject win32_service -Filter "name=`'$myService`'").ProcessID) | select StartTime

$timerunning = (get-date).Subtract($starttime.StartTime)

Q: Query filters are doing duplicated SQL A:

The main point I'd make is that the duplicated predicate is expected EF Core behavior, not something you should try to fix by making EF reuse the root Brand filter.

CarModel is independently queryable, so its query filter has to be applied whenever EF queries CarModel. EF cannot generally assume that because the outer Brand is filtered, every navigation to CarModel should inherit that result.

For the permission list, I'd also avoid putting a large AllowedResourceIds.Contains(...) collection directly into every entity query if this list can become large. A database-side permission table is usually a better design.

A concise answer could be:

The duplicated predicate is expected. EF Core applies a global query filter to each entity that participates in the query, including entities reached through a navigation. It does not try to infer that the Brand filter already guarantees the CarModel filter.

I would not try to make EF "reuse" the root filter. The bigger concern here is the size of AllowedResourceIds.

If the permission list can become large, consider storing the user's allowed resources in a table and doing a database-side join/EXISTS instead of generating a large IN (@p1, @p2, ...) predicate.

For example, conceptually:

WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM UserResourceAccess a
    WHERE a.UserId = @userId
      AND a.ResourceId = Brand.ResourceId
)

Then index the permission table appropriately, for example (UserId, ResourceId).

If the list is small, Contains()/IN is perfectly reasonable and I wouldn't optimize this prematurely.

For the specific query, you can also avoid navigating through CarModel -> Brand if the relationship already gives you the required BrandId, depending on what "active" means for your application.

So I'd separate the two issues:

  1. Repeated query-filter predicates are normal EF Core behavior.

  2. A large per-user resource list is the part I'd address architecturally, preferably with a database-side permission/ACL table rather than trying to make EF deduplicate the filters.

One thing I'd not claim is that query filters are inherently a bad choice for row-level security. They can be a good application-level guard. The question is whether the permission data should be represented as a large in-memory collection or as relational data that the database can index and join efficiently.

Q: Detect whether PowerShell scripts can be executed from Windows Batch A:

You can check it, but you probably shouldn't need to. The powershell.exe command line accepts an -ExecutionPolicy parameter that overrides the policy for that process only, without changing machine state and without requiring admin rights:

powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "C:\Users\username\file.ps1"

This makes your post-build event work on a fresh windows install out of the box, which is almost certainly what you actually want no dev onboarding step, no reminder message, no mutating global settings from a build script. -NoProfile is a good idea in build scripts anyway, so the build doesn't depend on whatever is in a dev's PowerShell profile.
If you still want to interrogate the policy from a batch file, Get-ExecutionPolicy is the counterpart to Set-ExecutionPolicy, and you can capture its output with for /f
